content: Vitamin D deficiency was historically a widespread condition affecting both children and adults, particularly in industrialized urban areas. The disease, known as rickets, was first scientifically described in the 17th century by British physicians. By the 20th century, German scientists had identified vitamin D and its critical role in bone health. The introduction of vitamin D fortification in milk during the 1930s significantly reduced the prevalence of rickets in the United States, making it a rare condition today. In 1645, Daniel Whistler, a British physician, provided the first scientific description of vitamin D deficiency in his thesis titled “Inaugural medical disputation on the disease of English children which is popularly termed the rickets,” submitted to the University of Leiden. Five years later, in 1650, Francis Glisson, a physician from Cambridge, published a detailed Latin text, “De Rachitide,” which meticulously documented his observations of children suffering from rickets. In 1918, Edward Mellanby discovered that cod liver oil had an antirachitic effect. By 1922, Elmer McCollum and his colleagues distinguished vitamin D from vitamin A and demonstrated its role in promoting calcium deposition in bones. In the 1930s, Adolf Otto Reinhold Windaus, a German chemist, elucidated the chemical structure of vitamin D and its precursor, 7-dehydrocholesterol. His groundbreaking work on sterols earned him the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1928. Several landmark events shaped the development of treatment strategies for rickets. In 1918, Mellanby successfully prevented rickets in puppies by administering cod liver oil. The following year, in 1919, Huldschinski observed that exposing children to radiation from a lamp had a therapeutic effect on rickets. In 1921, Hess and Unger conducted a study in New York City, exposing seven children with rickets to sunlight over several months, which resulted in significant improvement in their condition. However, in the 1950s, an outbreak of hypercalcemia in Great Britain led to the discontinuation of this program in Europe, though it remains in practice in the United States.
